title: Audit logging and accountability
summary: An audit log answers who did what, on whose authority, with which evidence and which versions. Log identifiers and decisions by default, keep content on a short, controlled leash, and make the accountability chain explicit.
useIf: You must reconstruct an agent's action, show a regulator what the system did, or assign accountability after an incident.
avoidIf: You plan to dump full prompts into a general log store: it copies protected content into a place with weaker access control.

explain.md: For high-risk systems, EU AI Act Article 12 requires the ability to record events automatically over the system's lifetime, supporting risk identification, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation [[r8]]. Deployers must keep the logs under their control for a period appropriate to the purpose, **at least six months**, unless other law, notably data protection law, provides otherwise [[tr1]]. OWASP recommends immutable retrieval logs for RAG [[tr10]].

**What to log** is a trade-off between debugging value and exposure. Default to identifiers and decisions: principal, agent identity, tool, argument hashes or ids, retrieved document ids, filter and policy decisions, model, prompt and tool versions, approver and outcome. Capture content only for a bounded window with its own access control, because logs copy ACL-protected content into a store that has no ACLs (design reasoning). **Accountability** needs a chain: the **sponsor** is accountable for purpose and lifecycle, the **owner** administers configuration and credentials, the agent identity acts, and in on-behalf-of mode a delegating user is a second identity to record [[r18]] [[r27]].

explain.title: The accountability chain in one record
explain.alt: A sponsor and owner govern an agent identity. A delegating user and an approver feed an action. The action produces an immutable audit record.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  SP[Sponsor] --> AG[Agent identity]
  OW[Owner] --> AG
  US[Delegating user] --> AG
  AG --> AC[Action]
  AP[Approver] --> AC
  AC --> LG[Audit record]

RAG retrieval layers, recording ids, principal and filter hash
Approval systems, recording who saw what evidence

Incident response, where logs decide containment and reporting

use: Actions affect people, money or data
A regulator, customer or auditor may ask for evidence
Several identities share responsibility for one action
You need to prove an approval happened
avoid: Logging raw content to a broadly readable store
Mutable logs that the acting system can edit
flips: Debugging needs content: capture it for a bounded window under its own ACL, then delete
Data-subject deletion applies: store ids and hashes, not personal content
Sampling would drop incidents: keep full audit records and sample only debug traces

pitfalls.symptom: A log search returns confidential documents to the wrong people
pitfalls.cause: Prompts and retrieved text were logged into a store without document-level access control
pitfalls.fix: Log ids and decisions, restrict content logs to a bounded window and a small group, and set retention

pitfalls.symptom: Nobody can tell which agent or user caused an action
pitfalls.cause: Only the service principal was logged, not the delegating user or approver
pitfalls.fix: Record agent identity, delegating user, sponsor and approver on every action

pitfalls.symptom: The incident window is missing from the logs
pitfalls.cause: Head sampling dropped the trace, or retention was too short
pitfalls.fix: Keep audit records unsampled and retain at least the legal minimum for your class

pitfalls.symptom: An investigator cannot trust the log
pitfalls.cause: The acting system can alter its own records
pitfalls.fix: Write to an append-only or immutable store with separate access

scenarios.title: A high-risk system in the EU
scenarios.situation: A deployer runs a system it has classified as high-risk. A regulator may ask what the system did on a given date.
unknowns: Which logs are under the deployer's control and which the provider keeps?
What retention period does the purpose justify?
scenarios.question: What do you keep?

options.name: Automatically generated event logs for at least six months in an immutable store, with ids and decisions, plus a documented retention rule
options.why: It meets the Article 26 floor and supports Article 12 purposes while limiting personal data.
options.tradeoff: Storage and governance cost, and some debugging detail is not available.

options.name: Keep full prompts and outputs forever
options.why: It collides with data-protection duties and enlarges the breach surface.
options.tradeoff: Right only where a rule demands content retention and access is tightly controlled.

options.name: Keep one month of logs to save cost
options.why: It is below the six-month minimum unless other law provides otherwise.
options.tradeoff: Shorter retention may be right for non-regulated systems.

flips.then: Choose retention by risk and business need.

flips.if: Another law sets a different period
flips.then: Follow it, and document the reason.

scenarios.takeaway: Six months is the floor for deployers of high-risk systems.

scenarios.title: An HR copilot over sensitive documents
scenarios.situation: An internal copilot answers questions over permissioned HR documents. Engineers want full prompt logs to debug retrieval.
unknowns: Who can read the log store?
Can a debug session be time boxed?
scenarios.question: What do you log?

options.name: Ids, principal, filter hash and decisions by default; content only for a time-boxed debug window with its own ACL
options.why: It keeps the audit trail and bounds the content copy.
options.tradeoff: Some debugging needs a ticket and a window.

options.name: Log everything to the shared platform log
options.why: It copies protected HR content into a store with broader readers.
options.tradeoff: Fine only for non-sensitive synthetic data.

options.name: Log nothing about content or retrieval
options.tradeoff: No evidence of what was retrieved, which weakens incident response.

flips.then: Extend the content window under approval.

scenarios.takeaway: Ids by default, content by exception.

scenarios.title: Many agents, one fleet
scenarios.situation: A fleet of agents acts on behalf of users and also autonomously. A customer disputes an action taken yesterday.
unknowns: Is there a correlation id across hand-offs?
Does the record include the approver?
scenarios.question: What must the record show?

options.name: Agent identity, delegating user if any, sponsor, approver, tool, argument ids, versions and a correlation id across hand-offs
options.why: It lets you attribute the action to people and versions and replay the chain.
options.tradeoff: More fields to populate and protect.

options.name: Service principal and timestamp only
options.why: Many agents share it, so accountability is lost.
options.tradeoff: Enough for a single trivial service.

options.name: Free-text log lines per agent
options.tradeoff: Hard to query, join or prove.

flips.then: Record the policy decision that allowed the action.

scenarios.takeaway: An unattributed action is an unaccountable action.

quiz.q: Under Article 26(6), what is the minimum period in months that deployers of high-risk systems keep automatically generated logs under their control, unless other law provides otherwise?
quiz.explain: Article 26(6) says a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, unless Union or national law (in particular data protection law) provides otherwise [[tr1]].

quiz.q: Which fields belong in a default audit record without copying protected content?
options: Retrieved document ids and filter decision
quiz.explain: Ids, decisions and versions support audit without copying content. Full passages belong only in a bounded, controlled debug window.

quiz.q: Why can verbose prompt logging create a data leak?
options: Logs copy ACL-protected content into a store with weaker access control
quiz.explain: The risk is access, not performance. Anyone with log access can read content they could not read in the source system.

flashcards.front: What do Article 12 and Article 26(6) require?
flashcards.back: Art 12: automatic event recording over the lifetime of high-risk systems. Art 26(6): deployers keep logs under their control at least six months unless other law differs.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable in the Entra Agent ID model?
flashcards.back: The sponsor is accountable for purpose and lifecycle, with at least one per agent identity. The owner administers configuration and credentials.

flashcards.front: Default content policy for audit logs?
flashcards.back: Ids and decisions by default. Content only for a bounded window with its own access control.
